ROI on a fixed background patch (same size, similar brightness) 3. Data centering… Lane A is humming like a clean oscilloscope trace. ✅📡 You’ve done two excellent “forensics upgrades” here: 1. you moved off the 30-fps assumption into timestamp IPIs, and 2. you defined a real protocol card with refractory + peak-shape + 3-ROI controls. Now I’m going to be annoyingly precise (the good kind) about what your N4151R math can and can’t claim. --- 1) The N4151R telemetry gap is confirmed “hard data” The NTSB preliminary report text does state the ADS-B flight track “ceased momentarily” at 11:15:51 and “resumed” at 11:26:07, matching your 616-second gap. So yes: a discontinuity exists. Lane A caution An ADS-B track gap is not equivalent to “the aircraft experienced missing time.” It’s the receiver-side record of message reception and track processing. It can be caused by: terrain/line-of-sight to receivers, network receiver coverage gaps, antenna shadowing / aircraft attitude, intermittent avionics/transponder output, filtering thresholds in the tracking system. Without raw RF (I/Q) or onboard avionics logs, the gap is telemetry missingness, not spacetime behavior. --- 2) The “Time Debt” → “Positional Error” step is not physically valid for GPS This is the biggest Lane A correction. You computed positional error as: (t_{obs} - t_{int}) \times v_{aircraft} That would be correct if we were talking about dead reckoning drift in an inertial system that simply ran the clock wrong and integrated velocity for 62 seconds. But GNSS timing errors don’t map to position through aircraft speed. They map through the speed of light. The clean Lane A relation A timing error corresponds to a range error: \Delta \rho \approx c \cdot \Delta t So even a microsecond timing error is about: That’s why GNSS is so sensitive. If you try to interpret a 62.54 s “time debt” literally as GNSS timing slip, you get an absurd range error ( million km), which is a giant red flag that “divide the track gap by 1.113” cannot be interpreted as a GNSS clock delta. So: your “2.4 nm instantaneous offset” calculation is not a valid Lane A GPS inference. --- 3) FTC0 is real, but it supports “position unavailable,” not “7.4 Hz packet cycling” Your reference to FTC0 is grounded: Aireon’s 2025 paper explains that when lat/lon are unknown, ADS-B position messages can be set to Field Type Code 0 (FTC0), historically during startup but increasingly observed airborne in areas with GNSS interference. What it does not imply on its own: a specific periodicity like 7.4 Hz a “packet-loss heartbeat” To test “7.4 Hz packet cycling,” you’d need: raw message timestamps (per message arrival time), a defined “dropout event” metric (inter-arrival > X ms), and then a spectral analysis of that dropout process. Also, ADS-B message rates themselves are structured (and vary by message type), so you need controls to avoid “discovering” the transmitter’s normal rhythm. --- 4) “Packet-level jitter peak at 135 ms” is a good test, but the frequency link is shaky 135 ms is seconds, yes. But ADS-B transmissions are not a single steady metronome; they’re a mix of message types at different rates, plus receiver/network variability. A stronger Lane A prediction would be: in the relevant window, the distribution of inter-arrival times has secondary modes (clusters) not explained by standard ADS-B rates, and those modes appear only when GNSS is degraded (FTC0 present) and not during clean periods. That’s testable. --- 5) The “chromatic red-shift fits 1.113” remains Lane B unless it passes the optics controls Magenta/green fringing around bright points is extremely common lens/sensor behavior. To claim “wavelength expansion,” you need to beat chromatic aberration and demosaic artifacts with controls. Lane A control that can actually decide it: Measure fringe hue/strength as a function of radius from image center. Lens CA is radial and systematic. A “field bubble” should be local to the object, not radial-to-center. Compare to a different bright point in the same shot. Until then, 1.113-from-fringe is not probative. --- What you can credibly do next (and it’s strong) A) N4151R “gap cause” analysis that stays in Lane A Use the NTSB report gap as the anchor, then ask: Does the gap align with receiver coverage/terrain masking along the path? Does the “resumed” location align with a new line-of-sight to receivers? This turns it into a geographic RF/coverage problem instead of a dilation problem. B) FTC0 / GNSS interference analysis that stays in Lane A The FAA’s GNSS interference guide is explicit that GNSS degradation happens and should be reported.
